row.basis: Rab as flock-owner and shepherd
row.note: The psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, giving the source's Rab who owns and directs the herd a direct divine pastoral frame.

row.basis: green pastures and resting waters
row.note: The shepherd brings the dependent flock to nourishing pasture and rest, closely matching the commentary's owner who brings the herd to a protected grazing place.

row.basis: restore and guide in right paths
row.note: The same shepherd restores and leads the person on paths; this makes the source's هدى B003 front-leading image part of pastoral care rather than mere travel.

row.basis: we are his; people and sheep of his pasture
row.note: The verse joins belonging to the creator with being the sheep of his pasture, directly combining the source's Rab-as-owner with its herd and grazing scene.

row.basis: cattle on a thousand hills are mine
row.note: God's claim over cattle supplies a concrete biblical form for the commentary's insistence that Rab is the owner before he is the herd's guide.

row.basis: ox knows owner; donkey its master's manger
row.note: Isaiah makes an animal's recognition of its owner and feeding-place a rebuke to Israel; it adds a reversal to the source's animal scene and its later naming of one's own Rab.

row.basis: green vegetation assigned as animal food
row.note: The creation decree gives green plants to land animals for food, a direct scriptural counterpart to God bringing forth pasture for livestock.

row.basis: grass for livestock and food for people
row.note: The land blessing explicitly moves from grass supplied for cattle to human eating, paralleling the commentary's pasture as provision for both people and their animals.

row.basis: grass for cattle; plants and food for humans
row.note: The psalm treats the sprouting of grass for cattle and human food as God's work, closely matching the source's creator of pasture and its 79:33 and 80:31 provision motif.

row.basis: rain makes grass grow on mountains
row.note: God covers the sky, prepares rain, and sprouts grass on the mountains; this connects divine production of grazing land with the commentary's mountain-and-pasture association.

row.basis: God gives food to beasts
row.note: The creator's provision of food to animals makes explicit the care for livestock that the source reads into pasture.

row.basis: leader goes before the people; sheep without shepherd
row.note: Moses asks for a successor who goes out before and brings in the congregation so it is not sheep without a shepherd; it directly joins the source's Musa setting, B003 leading-from-the-front, and ruler-as-shepherd.

row.basis: Moses and Aaron lead God's people like a flock
row.note: The psalm says God led the people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, giving the commentary's Moses-linked scene a divine owner, human agents, and flock in one verse.

row.basis: ruler commissioned to shepherd Israel
row.note: Israel tells David that he will shepherd God's people and be their ruler; its royal formula is a precise analogue to the source's B002 equation of governor and shepherd.

row.basis: God leads people as sheep and guides them as flock
row.note: The wilderness exodus is described with both flock-leading and guidance, closely matching the source's single work of owner, guide, and herd.

row.basis: David shepherds with integrity and skillful guidance
row.note: David's shepherding is defined by inner integrity and skilled leading, developing the source's claim that pastoral language can describe competent public rule.

row.basis: gather, carry, and gently lead the flock
row.note: The divine shepherd gathers vulnerable lambs, carries them, and gently leads nursing ewes; it gives concrete protective actions to the source's guarded pasture and leading owner.

row.basis: God gathers and keeps Israel as a shepherd
row.note: The one who scattered Israel gathers and guards it as a shepherd guards a flock, making protection and restoration integral to divine ownership.

row.basis: shepherd-rulers feed themselves instead of flock
row.note: Ezekiel's indictment turns the source's ruler-as-shepherd image into a negative test: leaders who consume provision themselves fail the flock entrusted to them.

row.basis: God gathers sheep and feeds them on mountains
row.note: God himself brings the scattered flock out, gathers it, and feeds it on the mountains; this is a particularly close scene of owner, leading, and pasture.

row.basis: good pasture and secure grazing land
row.note: The promised sheep receive good pasture and lie down in rich grazing land, supplying the protected-pasture element of the source without reducing it to a word match.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002/B003/B007; Hebrew רעה and מרעה
row.note: The Hebrew verb for tending and noun for pasture are cognate with the source's ر ع ي family; here they describe God feeding sheep in a good pasture, including both the source's shepherd and marʿā senses.

row.basis: God himself pastures and gives rest
row.note: The divine speaker personally shepherds the flock and makes it lie down, the clearest biblical formulation of the commentary's owner who both leads and supplies the grazing place.

row.basis: David appointed as one shepherd
row.note: God appoints David as the flock's shepherd, preserving the distinction between the ultimate owner and a commissioned human ruler developed in the source.

row.basis: pasture on every bare height
row.note: In the restoration promise, the released people feed along the ways and find pasture even on bare heights; it extends the source's pasture image into guided return and unexpected provision.

row.basis: guide to springs after hunger and thirst
row.note: The compassionate leader guides the redeemed to water after removing hunger and thirst, pairing direction with provision as the commentary does.

row.basis: ruler stands and shepherds in the LORD's strength
row.note: Micah joins rule, secure dwelling, and shepherding in the strength of God, a direct royal form of the source's ruler who tends his people.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002/B007; Hebrew רְעוּ pasture the flock
row.note: Jacob's well scene tells the herdsmen to water the flock and then go pasture it; the Hebrew cognate shows the source's ر ع ي family in an ordinary husbandry setting.

row.basis: grass withers when the LORD's breath blows
row.note: The grass fades under God's breath, furnishing a close biblical image for the source's pasture that is later made into dark debris and for its turn toward the temporary world.

row.basis: grass fades but God's word endures
row.note: The contrast between fading grass and what endures gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's move from temporary worldly provision to the better, lasting life.

row.basis: Moses carries the thirsty straying lamb
row.note: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate attention to a runaway lamb the reason God entrusts Israel to him; it turns the source's Musa-and-shepherd scene into a criterion for protective leadership.

row.basis: leader must go out and come in before Israel
row.note: The exposition of Numbers 27:17 reads Moses's request as one for a leader present with the people rather than distant from them, sharpening the source's image of the animal that leads the others from in front.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002; Aramaic rʿyā for shepherd
row.note: The Aramaic witness retains the congregation-as-sheep-without-a-shepherd image in Moses's succession request; its rʿyā is a cognate of the source's rāʿī and still carries public leadership.

row.basis: calls own sheep and leads them out
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, an unusually exact New Testament counterpart to the source's owner and B003 animal-leader scene.

row.basis: goes before sheep and they follow
row.note: The shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and they follow his known voice, directly realizing the commentary's detail of front animals guiding those behind.

row.basis: go in and out and find pasture
row.note: Within the shepherd discourse, entering through Jesus leads to safety and pasture; it joins protection with access to grazing as in the source's unified scene.

row.basis: good shepherd lays down life for sheep
row.note: The good shepherd's self-giving makes protection of the flock more radical than the source's lexical description of the shepherd who surrounds and preserves livestock.

row.basis: hired hand does not own sheep and abandons them
row.note: The contrast hinges on ownership and guarding: a hireling flees while the true shepherd's sheep are endangered, a negative foil to the source's owner who protects the herd.

row.basis: shepherd knows his own sheep
row.note: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep develops the source's closing move in which the person names this owner as his own Rab.

row.basis: ruler who will shepherd Israel
row.note: Matthew's citation calls the coming figure both ruler and shepherd of Israel, precisely echoing the source's ruler/shepherd equation.

row.basis: crowd as sheep without shepherd; Jesus teaches
row.note: Jesus responds to a shepherdless crowd by teaching it, making guidance of people the action expected from the missing shepherd.

row.basis: commission to shepherd my sheep
row.note: The risen Jesus entrusts his own sheep to Peter's care, distinguishing the flock's owner from the human leader who is commissioned to tend it.

row.basis: overseers shepherd God's acquired flock
row.note: The elders must watch over the whole flock and shepherd God's assembly; it makes pastoral rule explicitly attentive and accountable, resonating with B002 and the source's B003 watchfulness.

row.basis: return to shepherd and overseer of souls
row.note: Straying sheep return to a shepherd who is also an overseer, joining restoration, guidance, and supervisory care in the source's pastoral image.

row.basis: elders shepherd God's flock with oversight
row.note: The elders' charge makes shepherding a form of responsible oversight, giving a Christian communal application to the source's ruler who tends a people.

row.basis: chief shepherd appears
row.note: The title chief shepherd places local shepherd-leaders under a higher shepherd, akin to the source's distinction between the owner and those who lead within the herd scene.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life
row.note: The Lamb becomes the shepherd who guides the flock to living-water springs; it carries the source's pasture-and-guidance image into its own enduring, eschatological setting.

row.basis: ruling nations expressed by the shepherd verb
row.note: The royal judge's rule over nations is stated with the verb to shepherd, preserving the political sense of tending subjects foregrounded in source B002.

row.basis: all flesh like grass; grass withers
row.note: Peter applies fading grass to human mortality, a direct Christian extension of the source's pasture-to-debris and worldly-transience turn.

row.basis: word remains forever
row.note: The verse's enduring word completes the preceding grass image with a lasting contrast, comparable to the source's contrast between worldly life and what remains.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002; Syriac rʿyā, shepherd
row.note: The Peshitta's Syriac rʿyā for Jesus as the good shepherd is cognate with Arabic rāʿī in the source and uses the shared root for self-giving flock care.

row.basis: Moses pastures Jethro's flock to Horeb
row.note: The biblical Moses first appears at Horeb while tending and leading a flock; alongside the commentary's explicit Musa setting, this gives a concrete narrative pastoral setting without claiming the two accounts are the same scene.

row.basis: Moses protects shepherds and waters their flock
row.note: Moses drives away attackers and waters the flock for Midianite shepherds, a specific earlier portrayal of the protective action the source assigns to a shepherd.

row.basis: land belongs to God; people are temporary residents
row.note: God's ownership of land and the people's temporary tenancy give a land-based counterpart to the source's Rab-as-owner and its explanation of pasture as temporary metāʿ.

row.basis: Lord of sheep and accountable appointed shepherds
row.note: The Animal Apocalypse represents Israel as sheep under the Lord of the sheep and appointed shepherds whose stewardship is judged; it expands the source's owner, flock, and delegated leaders into an apocalyptic history.

row.basis: owner seeks the one lost sheep
row.note: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost sheep, making the source's enclosing and preserving shepherd an active seeker rather than only a keeper of pasture.

row.basis: Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: The title great shepherd binds communal pastoral imagery to the God of peace and resurrection, a Christian theological development of the source's divine owner/shepherd.

row.basis: grass today, cast into an oven tomorrow
row.note: Jesus uses grass's brief life to teach trust in God's provision; the image closely meets the source's created pasture that soon changes, while its argument concerns anxious humans rather than livestock.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 46
row.basis: Christ as good shepherd versus hireling
row.note: Augustine's exposition of John 10 reads the good shepherd's care and self-giving as Christological, giving a major Christian interpretive frame for the owner, flock, and protective contrast in the source.

row.basis: angel of repentance appears as shepherd
row.note: Hermas receives moral commands from a shepherd figure; this later Christian use turns pastoral guidance into corrective formation, a plausible extension of the source's Rab-as-corrector within its herd image.

row.basis: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: The verse makes Israel both God's people and the sheep held in his hand; its call to hear his voice joins ownership, pastoral care, and responsive recognition of the Rab.

row.basis: Shepherd of Israel leads Joseph like a flock
row.note: The invocation directly addresses God as Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph as a flock, concentrating the source's owner and front-leading functions.

row.basis: shepherd and carry God's inheritance forever
row.note: The plea asks God to save, bless, shepherd, and carry his people forever; it makes protective pastoral rule explicitly enduring, relevant to the source's turn from temporary pasture to what lasts.

row.basis: God has shepherded Jacob all his life
row.note: Jacob calls God the one who has been his shepherd throughout life, giving the source's personal naming of one's Rab a concentrated ancestral precedent.

row.basis: flock of God's pasture gives thanks forever
row.note: The flock-of-your-pasture formula culminates in perpetual thanksgiving; it brings the source's opening glorification of the Rab into the pastoral relation itself.

row.basis: David taken from pasture and following sheep to rule Israel
row.note: God recalls taking David from following sheep to be prince over Israel, making the shepherd-to-ruler transition explicit rather than merely metaphorical.

row.basis: David pursues a predator and rescues the lamb
row.note: David's shepherding includes going after the lion or bear and delivering the sheep from its mouth, a concrete protective action for the source's keeper who guards livestock.

row.basis: shepherd bears loss for animals torn or stolen
row.note: Jacob describes accepting liability for flock losses rather than passing them to the owner; this gives a demanding economic form to the source's protective shepherd.

row.basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
row.note: The instruction requires sustained, informed attention to a herd, closely matching the source's B003 extension from shepherding to watching where a matter is going.

row.basis: old grass passes and new growth appears
row.note: The pastoral maxim traces hay's disappearance, fresh growth, and mountain vegetation; it offers a close agrarian counterpart to pasture brought forth and then transformed.

row.basis: rain, abundant bread, and livestock grazing broad pasture
row.note: The promised divine rain produces abundance and broad pasture for cattle, directly matching the commentary's creator who produces grazing provision for people and animals.

row.basis: working oxen and donkeys eat prepared fodder
row.note: Farm animals receive rich fodder while doing agricultural work, a close counterpart to the source's B007 detail of working animals grazing around a settled community.

row.basis: Moses gives water to congregation and livestock
row.note: God instructs Moses to bring water from the rock for both the people and their animals; it is a specific Mosaic scene of shared human-and-livestock provision.

row.basis: just rule in the fear of God
row.note: David's oracle defines the God-fearing ruler whose effect is developed in the next verse; it supplies the governing member of the source's shepherd-ruler image.

row.basis: rain causes grass to sprout from the earth
row.note: The next line compares the just ruler's advent to light and rain that sprouts grass, a striking joining of righteous rule with the growth of the source's pasture.

row.basis: pastures clothed with flocks and fields sing
row.note: Pastures are filled with flocks and the fertile landscape shouts and sings; it lets the source's opening praise encompass the very pasture and herd that God causes to thrive.

row.basis: evil-doers sprout like grass only for destruction
row.note: The psalm uses flourishing grass for a short-lived prosperity that ends in destruction, closely paralleling the source's pasture that becomes debris and its warning about transient life.

row.basis: the Most High is forever
row.note: The contrast calls YHWH the Most High forever, joining the source's al-Aʿlā title to its contrast between fading grass and enduring reality.

row.basis: wise instruction given by one shepherd
row.note: Ecclesiastes attributes wisdom that prods and steadies its hearers to one shepherd, extending the source's pastoral guide into correction and instruction.

row.basis: failed shepherds do not strengthen, heal, bind, seek, or restore
row.note: The detailed catalogue says what pastoral rule owes the vulnerable flock; it concretizes the source's claim that the shepherd surrounds and preserves those in his care.

row.basis: God seeks lost, restores strayed, binds injured, and strengthens weak
row.note: God's own response reverses failed leadership through specific acts of search, restoration, and healing, deepening the source's owner-protector scene.

row.basis: human sheep of God's pasture
row.note: The chapter's conclusion explicitly calls the people God's sheep and flock of his pasture, completing the source's owner, people, and grazing-place relation.

row.basis: shepherds after God's heart feed knowledge and understanding
row.note: God promises leaders who feed the people with knowledge and discernment, making pastoral governance an intellectual and moral guidance like the source's leading function.

row.basis: shepherds lead sheep astray from their resting place
row.note: The lost sheep are misdirected by their shepherds through the mountains and forget their resting place; this is a pointed negative reversal of the source's guide who brings a flock to pasture.

row.basis: shepherd rescues remnants from a lion's mouth
row.note: Amos's image of a shepherd recovering only a leg or ear from a predator gives a grim, concrete limit case for the source's protecting shepherd.

row.basis: foolish shepherd neither seeks, heals, nor nourishes
row.note: The false shepherd neglects the lost and injured and consumes the fat flock instead; this negative portrait tests every protective and provisioning element developed in the source.

row.basis: grazing leads to fullness, pride, and forgetting the owner
row.note: Hosea depicts pasture and fullness producing self-exaltation and forgetfulness of God, an ethical counterpoint to the source's pasture as temporary provision under its owner.

row.basis: Davidic king shepherds the Lord's flock faithfully
row.note: The psalm portrays the hoped-for Davidic ruler as faithfully shepherding the Lord's flock, preventing their stumbling in pasture and leading them in holiness; it fuses delegated rule, divine ownership, and guidance.

row.basis: eternal life and no snatching from the shepherd's hand
row.note: Jesus gives the sheep unending life and guarantees that no one will snatch them away, bringing the source's guarded flock and its lasting-life contrast together.

row.basis: fierce wolves will not spare the flock
row.note: Paul's warning supplies the threat that makes pastoral watchfulness necessary, sharpening the source's protective shepherd rather than repeating its generic title.

row.basis: leaders do not dominate but become examples to the flock
row.note: The elders are forbidden to lord it over those entrusted to them and instead model conduct; it qualifies the source's ruler-shepherd relation with a specific non-dominating form of leadership.

row.basis: flock no longer hungers or thirsts
row.note: The eschatological community's freedom from hunger and thirst supplies the provision that the following shepherd-and-springs image brings to completion, echoing the source's pasture and lasting-life movement.

row.basis: pastors joined with teachers in communal leadership
row.note: The risen Christ gives pastors-and-teachers to the community, a concise Christian institutional use of shepherd language for guiding and forming people.

row.basis: Paul rereads the unmuzzled ox command for apostolic support
row.note: Paul cites the Torah's feeding of a working ox and asks how its principle bears on apostolic workers; this is a deliberate interpretive reapplication of animal provision, not simply a duplicate pasture image.

row.basis: the world passes away while the doer of God's will remains
row.note: The verse gives a direct Christian formulation of the source's distinction between the passing worldly life reached through temporary provision and what endures.

row.basis: riches and crown do not endure
row.note: Following the flock-watch instruction, the proverb states that wealth and political standing are not permanent; its own transience claim clarifies why the source calls pasture provision temporary metāʿ.

row.basis: working ox must not be muzzled
row.note: The law protects an animal's access to food while it works, a concrete ethical analogue to the source's working camels and livestock sustained by grazing.

row.basis: camels receive straw and fodder at a household
row.note: The servant's camels are unloaded and supplied with straw and fodder at the house, a specific narrative counterpart to the source's camels grazing around people and dwellings.

row.basis: God makes grass sprout in desolate ground
row.note: God satisfies wasteland and makes grass grow where people do not cultivate it; this extends the source's pasture-maker to nonhuman and wild terrain.

row.basis: God declares the end from the beginning
row.note: The source explicitly makes the pasture's maker one who sees what it will become; Isaiah's divine knowledge of end from beginning is a precise theological bridge for that secondary claim.

row.basis: a child leads reconciled wild and domestic animals
row.note: The future peace scene gives a child the action of leading a mixed animal company, an indirect but specific counterpart to the source's B003 image of a leader before other animals.

row.basis: cow and bear graze; lion eats straw like ox
row.note: The transformed creation is pictured through shared grazing and fodder among animals, a distinct eschatological extension of the source's pasture and livestock scene.

row.basis: the righteous knows an animal's needs
row.note: The proverb makes attentive care for an animal a mark of righteousness, giving an ethical consequence to the source's shepherd who protects livestock.

row.basis: one who tends a flock shares its milk
row.note: Paul's pastoral labor analogy assumes that the flock's keeper receives its produce, linking the source's pasture as provision with the work of tending it.

row.basis: plowman and thresher work in hope of a share
row.note: Paul states the human-worker application of the ox text: laborers should expect a share of the yield. It reframes the source's livestock provision as a principle about those who serve a community.

row.basis: little flock and the Father's gift of the kingdom
row.note: Jesus calls the disciples a little flock while locating their security in the Father's gift of the kingdom, joining pastoral belonging with the source's movement beyond temporary worldly provision.

row.basis: seen things are temporary and unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul's temporal-eternal contrast is a close Christian formulation of the source's conclusion about the worldly life and the more enduring reality, though it does not itself use pasture imagery.

row.basis: shepherd separates sheep from goats at judgment
row.note: The final judgment is pictured through a shepherd sorting a mixed herd; it gives the source's animal scene an eschatological use distinct from provisioning and protection.

row.basis: struck shepherd and scattered sheep
row.note: The passion prediction reverses the source's secure owner-and-flock scene: when the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter, showing the flock's dependence on its guide.

row.basis: lost largest sheep sought over the ninety-nine
row.note: This Christian apocryphal version makes the wandering sheep the largest and specially loved one; it is a distinctive reception of the owner who actively seeks and values a member of the flock.
